title: Hollow Hourglass Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: gap-rim-edge per-cell checks versus classifying each row once and building its star region directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer n, print an hourglass shape with 2n minus 1 rows, where the very top and bottom rows are completely solid, and every row in between is hollow, only its two edges are stars, narrowing down to a single star in the exact middle.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print an hourglass shape with 2n minus 1 rows, where the very top and bottom rows are completely solid, and every row in between is hollow, only its two edges are stars, narrowing down to a single star in the exact middle.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Real Glass Hourglass
blocks.text: Picture an actual sand timer, where the thick glass rim at the very top and very bottom is completely solid, but the tapering sides of the glass in between are just a thin outline, hollow all the way down to the narrow neck in the middle where the two hollow cones meet.

blocks.caption: The top and bottom rims are solid, every row between them is hollow

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","*******","m is 1, the top rim, so the entire width 7 star region is solid, not hollow."],["Row 2"," *   *","m is 2, a hollow row, one space of gap and a star, three hollow spaces, a star."],["Row 3","  * *","m is 3, a hollow row, two spaces of gap, star, one hollow space, star."],["Row 4","   *","m is 4, the pinch point, three spaces of gap and exactly one star, too narrow to hollow out."],["Row 5","  * *","m is 3 again, measured from the bottom edge, matching row 3 as the shape widens back out."],["Row 6"," *   *","m is 2, continuing to widen toward the bottom rim."],["Row 7","*******","m is 1, the bottom rim, solid again, matching row 1."]]}

blocks.text: With n = 1, the top and bottom rims collapse into a single row, a single star.
No rows at all, so nothing is printed.

This shape looks like a brand new combination, but it is worth checking exactly how the hollow pyramid's special solid-row idea needs to change when applied to a shape that mirrors itself around a middle point instead of ending at a base.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The distance measurement and the growing-gap, shrinking-star formula here are exactly the same ones already used for the plain hourglass.

Observation 2: The hollow pyramid had exactly one special solid row, its base, at the very end of the shape. This shape is symmetric around a middle point instead of ending at a base, so wherever that pyramid had one special end, this shape has two, the top rim and the bottom rim.

Observation 3: Testing a small example, n equal to 4, confirms it: both row 1 and row 7, the two rows where m equals 1, need to be completely solid, while every row in between, including the pinch point, follows the hollow edge only rule.

Observation 4: Once that doubled special case is identified, m equal to 1 means solid, everything else means hollow, the same edge only construction from the hollow pyramid still builds every non rim row directly.

The key adjustment here is not a new technique at all, it is recognizing that a special case which appeared once in an earlier, one ended shape must appear twice in a shape that mirrors itself around a middle point.

For every row, first work out its distance from the nearer edge, top or bottom, then check every column individually, printing a space while still in the leading gap, and afterward deciding whether this row is a solid rim or a hollow row that only fills in its two edges.

items: Loop over every row r, from 1 to 2n minus 1.
Compute m, the distance of this row from whichever edge is closer.
Compute the gap and the star region width from m.
For each column, print a space while still in the gap.
Once past the gap, print a star everywhere if this is the top or bottom rim, otherwise print a star only at the first or last position of the star region.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check the gap, then the rim condition, then the edge position

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: m, gap, and stars are computed once per row using the same formulas as the plain hourglass, before the inner loop even begins.
The check for m equal to 1, the rim condition, is repeated for every single column in that row, even though it is a row level fact that never changes within the row.
The edge check, k equal to 0 or k equal to stars minus 1, is also re-evaluated per column, even though only two specific positions in a non rim row will ever satisfy it.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every column position is checked against the gap, the rim condition, and the edge condition before deciding what to print.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the total width across all rows is proportional to n squared, and every position gets its own multi part check.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: the row type, whether this is a solid rim or a hollow row between them, is already known before the row even starts, so there is no need to re-check it for every single column. The whole star region for a row can be built directly in one operation, either fully solid or just its two edges, without visiting each position individually.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: the row-level fact, is this a rim row, m equal to 1, gets re-checked once per column instead of once per row.

What stays the same as two earlier problems: the growing-gap, shrinking-star formula from the plain hourglass, and the edge only construction from the hollow pyramid.

What is different here: the hollow pyramid's single special solid row, the base, becomes TWO special solid rows here, the top rim and the bottom rim, both occurring wherever m equals 1.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, a solid repeat operation still builds a rim row in one step, and a star-gap-star construction still builds every hollow row in between.

The core idea: classify each row once as a rim, m equal to 1, or hollow, everything else, then build its star region directly and attach the leading gap.

For each row, decide once whether it is the solid rim or a hollow row between the two rims. Build the star region directly, either a solid run of stars for the rim, or a star, a gap of spaces, and a star for every other row, then attach the leading gap and print the whole row with one call.
For each row, decide once whether it is the solid rim or a hollow row, then build the star region directly, attach the leading gap, and print the row once.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: decide the row type once, build the star region directly

blocks.text: This works because a row's classification, rim or hollow, depends only on whether m equals 1, and once that classification is made, the star region's exact shape is fully determined; a direct repeat operation constructs the solid rim in one step, and a star-gap-star construction, or a lone star at the width 1 pinch point, builds every other row just as directly. Because m equals 1 at both r equal to 1 and r equal to 2n minus 1, this same single condition automatically produces the solid rim at both extremes, with no need to check r directly against either end.

items: m, gap, and stars are computed once per row using the same formulas as the plain hourglass.
The single condition m equal to 1 classifies a row as a rim, automatically catching both r equal to 1 and r equal to 2n minus 1 without checking either end directly.
Every other row is built as a star-gap-star construction, or a lone star when stars equals 1 at the pinch point, the exact same edge only technique already used for the hollow pyramid.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with a single row-type decision per row instead of a per cell check, and O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared).
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Build all 7 rows","\"*******\", \" *   *\", \"  * *\", \"   *\", \"  * *\", \" *   *\", \"*******\"","Each row is still built directly from its own classification and lengths, independent of the others."],["Join with newlines","All 7 rows joined into one string","Joining every row in advance assembles the complete hollow hourglass, with its two solid rims, as a single string before any output happens."],["Print once","The full pattern appears in one call","A single output call now produces the entire hollow hourglass, regardless of how many rows it has."]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly from its own classification and lengths, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is collecting each finished row instead of printing it immediately.
Joining all 2n minus 1 rows with newline characters assembles the complete hollow hourglass, including both solid rims, as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole shape, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: This shape combines the solid special row idea from the hollow pyramid with the narrowing gap and star count from the plain hourglass, except here the special solid rows sit at both extremes rather than at just one end, since an hourglass mirrors itself around its narrow middle.

items: Making only one rim solid, forgetting that both the very top and very bottom rows need the same solid treatment.
Applying the hollow edge rule to the pinch point at the middle, where the star region is already just one star with nothing to hollow out.
Reusing the plain hourglass formula without adding the rim special case, leaving every row solid instead of hollow.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n = 0","Produces an empty pattern with no output."],["n = 1","The top and bottom rims collapse into a single row, a single star."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating which rows are the special solid cases, here both extremes rather than just one, before writing the general formula avoids a common source of off by one style mistakes in shapes that mirror themselves around a center point.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how is this different from the hollow pyramid's special row", think: a shape mirrored around its middle needs that same special case applied at both extremes, not just one.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every cell", think: classify the row as rim or hollow once, using m equal to 1, then build it directly.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

The plain hourglass, whose distance measurement and growing-gap, shrinking-star formula are reused here unchanged.
The hollow pyramid, whose solid special-row idea and edge only construction are both reused here, just doubled to apply at both extremes.
The hollow butterfly, which reuses the same edge only construction technique but for two side by side wings instead of a top to bottom taper.
Any shape that mirrors around a center point, where a special case discovered at one end of a related, one ended shape usually needs to be applied at both ends here.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: multi part per cell checks in the brute force version, one row-type decision per row in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: hollow shape printing that combines the special solid-row idea from the hollow pyramid with the plain hourglass's growing gap and shrinking star count, except here the special solid rows sit at both extremes rather than at just one end.

Core Idea: classify each row as a rim, when m equals 1, or hollow otherwise, using the same distance measurement as the plain hourglass, then build the rim as a solid run and every hollow row as a star-gap-star construction, or a lone star at the pinch point.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: a special case that appears once in a one ended shape typically needs to appear twice in a shape that mirrors around its middle.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape by adapting the plain hourglass; explicitly naming the doubled special case is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: hourglass's distance formula, hollow pyramid's edge rule, solid rim wherever m equals 1.
